name: Node.js & Express
description: Build back-end servers and REST APIs with JavaScript using Node.js, Express and MongoDB.

blocks.html:
Introduction & Modules

What is Node.js?

Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside the browser. It uses the V8 engine, the same engine that runs JavaScript in Chrome, and adds tools for things a browser is not allowed to do: reading files, opening network ports and talking to databases. This makes Node.js a popular choice for building back-end servers and APIs.

The big advantage is that you use one language for the whole project. Your React or plain JavaScript front end and your Node.js back end can both be written in JavaScript.

You run a file with the command node app.js. There is no browser, so there is no document or window. Instead you get Node tools such as node:fs for files and node:http for servers.

The event loop

Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so it does one thing at a time. Yet a Node server can handle thousands of users. The trick is that slow work, such as reading a file or waiting for a database, is handed to the system. When the work is finished, the event loop picks up your callback and runs it. Node never sits idle waiting.

The demo shows the order. Normal code runs first. Then promise callbacks run. Timers run after that, even when the delay is 0.

blocks.output:
1. start
2. end of file
3. promise callback
4. timer callback

blocks.html:
ES modules: import and export

Real programs are split into many files. Each file is a module. In modern Node.js we use ES modules, the same import and export syntax you see in front-end code. Put "type": "module" in package.json to turn them on for .js files.

  • A named export is imported with curly braces: import { area } from './math.js'.
  • A default export is imported without braces, and you may choose any name.
  • For your own files you must write the extension, for example ./math.js.

blocks.output:
Hello, Ali!
Area of a circle with r = 2: 12.56636

blocks.html:
ES modules and CommonJS

Older Node code uses CommonJS: require() to load and module.exports to share. You will meet it in old tutorials. Files ending in .cjs are always CommonJS and files ending in .mjs are always ES modules. Built-in modules are best imported with the node: prefix, like node:fs, so it is clear they come from Node.

blocks.output:
$ node old-style.cjs
function object
string
$ node new-style.mjs
undefined string
string

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Using import in a project without "type": "module". Node then says "Cannot use import statement outside a module".
  • Forgetting the .js extension in import ... from './math'.
  • Using document or alert in Node. They only exist in browsers.
  • Mixing require and import in the same file.

Key Points

  • Node.js runs JavaScript on the server using the V8 engine.
  • One thread plus the event loop handles many requests without waiting.
  • Use ES modules: export, import and "type": "module".
  • Import built-in modules with the node: prefix.
  • CommonJS (require) is the older style.

npm & the File System

npm and package.json

npm is the package manager that comes with Node.js. It downloads code written by other developers, called packages, so you do not have to write everything yourself. Every Node project has a file called package.json. It holds the project name, the scripts you can run, and the list of packages the project needs.

Start a new project with npm init -y. The -y flag accepts all the default answers. Then use npm pkg set to add the settings we need: ES modules and a start script.

blocks.code:
mkdir my-app
cd my-app
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set scripts.start="node index.js"
cat package.json
blocks.output:
$ mkdir my-app
$ cd my-app
$ npm init -y

{
  "name": "my-app",

blocks.html:
Installing packages

Run npm install express to add a package. npm downloads it into a folder called node_modules, adds it under dependencies in package.json, and records exact versions in package-lock.json. Packages that you only need while developing, like a test tool, are installed with npm install -D name.

A script in package.json is run with npm run name. The special name start can be run as npm start. The exact numbers below can differ on your computer.

blocks.code:
npm install express
npm run start
blocks.output:
$ npm install express
added 65 packages, and audited 66 packages in 4s

30 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
$ npm run start
> my-app@1.0.0 start
> node index.js

Hello from my-app!

blocks.html: After the install, package.json has a new section:

What goes in Git?

ItemWhat it isCommit to Git?
package.jsonname, scripts, dependenciesYes
package-lock.jsonexact installed versionsYes
node_modules/downloaded packagesNo
.envsecrets and settingsNo

Anyone can rebuild node_modules by running npm install, so put node_modules and .env in a .gitignore file.

Reading and writing files

Node can work with files through node:fs/promises. Its functions return promises, so we use await. The most useful ones are readFile, writeFile and readdir. Pass 'utf8' to readFile to get text instead of raw bytes.

The node:path module builds file paths safely on any operating system. Never join paths with plain string plus, because Windows uses \ and Linux uses /. In an ES module, import.meta.dirname is the folder of the current file. File operations can fail, for example when a file does not exist, so wrap them in try/catch. The error has a code such as ENOENT (no such file).

blocks.output:
Read from notes.txt
Buy milk
Learn Express

Extension: .txt
Name only: notes
Joined: data/users/ali.json
Error code: ENOENT
[ 'fs-demo.js', 'notes.txt', 'package.json' ]

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Committing node_modules or .env to Git.
  • Forgetting await, which gives you a Promise instead of the file text.
  • Using a relative path like 'notes.txt'. It depends on where you ran node from. Build the path from import.meta.dirname.

Key Points

  • npm init -y creates package.json.
  • npm install name adds a package; -D is for development tools.
  • npm run name runs a script; npm start is a shortcut.
  • Do not commit node_modules or .env.
  • Use node:fs/promises with await and node:path for file work.

HTTP & a First Server

How the web talks: HTTP

Browsers and servers talk using HTTP. The conversation is always the same: the client sends a request, and the server sends back a response. Nothing happens until a client asks.

A request has a method (what to do), a URL (which thing), headers and sometimes a body. A response has a status code, headers and a body.

MethodMeaning
GETread data
POSTcreate new data
PUTupdate data
DELETEremove data
StatusMeaning
200OK
201Created
400Bad request (client sent wrong data)
404Not found
500Server error (a bug on our side)

Your first server

Node has an HTTP server built in, in the node:http module. You call http.createServer() and give it a function. Node runs that function for every request and passes two objects: req (the request) and res (the response).

  • req.method and req.url tell you what the client asked for.
  • res.writeHead(status, headers) sets the status code and headers.
  • res.end(body) sends the body and finishes the response.

Then server.listen(3000) makes the server wait for connections on port 3000. The program keeps running until you press Ctrl+C. The demo starts the server in one terminal and uses curl, a command line HTTP client, in a second terminal.

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node server.js
Server running on http://localhost:3000
GET /
GET /api/time
GET /nothing

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s localhost:3000/
Welcome to my first server
$ echo
$ curl -s localhost:3000/api/time
{"ok":true,"message":"JSON from node:http"}
$ echo
$ curl -s -w "status: %{http_code}\n" localhost:3000/nothing
Page not foundstatus: 404

blocks.html:
Looking closer

Look at the server terminal. It printed one line for every request, and the 404 page was returned for a URL we did not handle. We chose to answer /api/time with JSON, the text format that front-end code and other servers understand. We set the Content-Type header to application/json so the client knows how to read the body.

This works, but you can already see the problem. Every new page needs another if. Reading a JSON body, parsing query strings and handling many routes would become long and messy. That is why almost everyone uses a framework on top of node:http. In the next section we meet Express.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting res.end(). The browser keeps waiting and never finishes loading.
  • Calling res.end() twice, or writing headers after the body has started.
  • Starting the server twice on the same port. Node shows an EADDRINUSE error. Stop the old one first.
  • Editing the code and expecting the running server to change. Stop it with Ctrl+C and start it again.

Key Points

  • HTTP is request and response: method, URL, headers, body, status code.
  • http.createServer((req, res) => { ... }) runs once per request.
  • Always finish with res.end().
  • Set Content-Type so the client understands the body.
  • Plain node:http gets long, so we use Express.

Express Routing

Why Express?

Express is a small framework that sits on top of Node's HTTP server. It gives you a clean way to say: "when a GET request arrives for this URL, run this function". These lessons use Express 5. Install it with npm install express.

A route has three parts: the HTTP method, a path, and a handler function. For example app.get('/', (req, res) => { ... }). There is one method per HTTP verb: app.get, app.post, app.put, app.delete.

Reading data from the request

Clients can send data in three common ways.

WhereExample URL or requestWhere you read it
Route parameterGET /users/42req.params.id
Query stringGET /search?q=nodereq.query.q
JSON bodyPOST /echoreq.body

A path like /users/:id has a parameter. The part after the colon becomes a key in req.params. Values from the URL are always strings, so '42' not 42. To read a JSON body, you must first add app.use(express.json()). We will see why in the next lesson.

To reply, use res.send() for text, res.json() for JSON, and res.status(201) to set the status code. You can chain them: res.status(201).json({ ... }).

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node app.js
Listening on 3000

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/'
Hello from Express  [200]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/users/42'
{"id":"42"}  [200]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/search?q=node&page=2'
{"query":{"q":"node","page":"2"}}  [200]
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ali"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/echo
{"youSent":{"name":"Ali"}}  [201]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/files/special'
special route wins (it is first)  [200]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/files/report'
file: report  [200]

blocks.html:
Order matters

Express checks routes from top to bottom and uses the first one that matches. In the demo, /files/special is written before /files/:name, so the special route wins. If we swapped them, :name would match special first. Always put specific routes before general ones.

If no route matches, Express sends a 404 response by itself. You can also group routes in a Router (express.Router()) and mount it with app.use('/api', router). This keeps big projects tidy.

Common mistakes

  • Reading req.body without express.json(). It is undefined in Express 5.
  • Forgetting that req.params.id is a string. Use Number(req.params.id) when comparing with numbers.
  • Sending two responses in one handler. After res.json(), use return if more code follows.
  • Putting a general route like /:name above specific ones.

Key Points

  • A route is a method, a path and a handler: app.get(path, handler).
  • req.params holds :id values, req.query holds ?key=value, req.body holds JSON.
  • Reply with res.send, res.json and res.status.
  • Routes are tested top to bottom; the first match wins.

Middleware

What is middleware?

Middleware is a function that runs between the request arriving and the response leaving. It receives (req, res, next). It can read or change req and res, and then it does one of two things: call next() to pass the request on, or send a response and stop.

Think of a security gate at a university. Each guard checks something. If all guards are happy, you reach the classroom. If one guard says no, you are turned away at that gate.

Using middleware

  • app.use(fn) runs fn for every request, in the order you wrote it.
  • app.get('/private', fn, handler) runs fn only for that one route.
  • Built-in helpers are middleware too: express.json() reads a JSON body and fills req.body.

The demo has a logger that prints every request, and requireKey that checks a header. Notice return res.status(401).... When middleware sends a response, it does not call next(), so the route handler never runs.

The last middleware has four parameters: (err, req, res, next). That is how Express knows it is the error handler. When any handler throws an error, Express skips to the error handler. In Express 5, errors thrown inside async handlers, or rejected promises, are also sent there automatically.

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node app.js
Listening on 3000
GET /public
GET /private
GET /private
POST /boom
Error caught: Something broke

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/public'
{"message":"anyone can see this"}  [200]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/private'
{"error":"Missing or wrong API key"}  [401]
$ curl -s -H 'x-api-key: secret123' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/private'
{"message":"welcome in"}  [200]
$ curl -s -X POST -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/boom
{"error":"Something broke"}  [500]

blocks.html:
Order matters again

Middleware runs in the order you add it. This is the most common source of bugs. In the next demo, express.json() is added after the /a route. So /a does not get a parsed body, but /b does. Always register express.json() near the top.

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node app.js
Listening on 3000

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"x":1}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/a'
{"body":"undefined"}  [200]
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"x":1}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/b'
{"body":{"x":1}}  [200]

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to call next(). The request hangs because nothing sends a response.
  • Calling next() after already sending a response.
  • Registering express.json() after the routes that need it.
  • Writing an error handler with three parameters. It must have exactly four.
  • Placing the error handler before the routes. It should come last.

Key Points

  • Middleware has the shape (req, res, next).
  • Call next() to continue, or send a response to stop.
  • app.use() applies to all routes; add middleware before a handler for one route.
  • Order of registration is the order of execution.
  • An error handler has four parameters and goes last.

Building a REST API

What is REST?

A REST API is a set of URLs that a front end can call to work with data. The URLs name things (resources) like books or users, and the HTTP method says the action. This pattern is called CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete.

ActionMethodURLSuccess
List allGET/api/books200
Read oneGET/api/books/:id200
CreatePOST/api/books201
UpdatePUT/api/books/:id200
DeleteDELETE/api/books/:id204

Use plural nouns in URLs (/api/books), never verbs like /api/getBooks. Always return JSON.

Good status codes and validation

A good API tells the client clearly what happened. Return 201 after creating something, 204 (no body) after deleting, 400 when the client sent bad data, and 404 when the item does not exist. Never trust incoming data. Check the required fields before you save.

The demo below keeps books in a plain array. This is a good way to practise before adding a real database. The data is lost when the server restarts. Read the output step by step: create, read, update, delete, and what each status code says.

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node app.js
Books API on port 3000

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/api/books'
[{"id":1,"title":"Clean Code","author":"Robert Martin"},{"id":2,"title":"Eloquent JavaScript","author":"Marijn Haverbeke"}]  [200]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/api/books/2'
{"id":2,"title":"Eloquent JavaScript","author":"Marijn Haverbeke"}  [200]
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Node in Action","author":"Mike Cantelon"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/api/books
{"id":3,"title":"Node in Action","author":"Mike Cantelon"}  [201]
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"No author"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/api/books
{"error":"title and author are required"}  [400]
$ curl -s -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Clean Code, 2nd ed"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/api/books/1
{"id":1,"title":"Clean Code, 2nd ed","author":"Robert Martin"}  [200]
$ curl -s -X DELETE -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/api/books/2
  [204]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/api/books/2'
{"error":"Book not found"}  [404]
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/api/books'
[{"id":1,"title":"Clean Code, 2nd ed","author":"Robert Martin"},{"id":3,"title":"Node in Action","author":"Mike Cantelon"}]  [200]

blocks.html:
Understanding the code

  • Number(req.params.id) turns the string from the URL into a number, so it matches the numeric id.
  • return res.status(404)... stops the handler early when the book is missing.
  • PUT uses ?? so only the fields that were sent are changed.
  • DELETE answers 204 with res.status(204).end(), because there is nothing to send back.

You can test an API like this with curl, with a tool such as Postman, or with fetch() from front-end code. Later we will replace the array with MongoDB. The routes stay almost the same; only the lines that touch the data change.

Common mistakes

  • Returning 200 for everything, even errors.
  • Forgetting validation, so a missing title gets saved.
  • Using the wrong type: b.id === req.params.id compares a number with a string and never matches.
  • Using verbs in URLs instead of the HTTP method.
  • Forgetting express.json(), so req.body is undefined.

Key Points

  • REST uses URLs for things and HTTP methods for actions.
  • CRUD maps to POST, GET, PUT and DELETE.
  • Use correct status codes: 200, 201, 204, 400, 404, 500.
  • Validate input and return JSON error messages.

MongoDB & Mongoose

What is MongoDB?

MongoDB is a NoSQL database. Instead of tables with rows and columns, it stores documents that look like JSON objects, grouped into collections. Every document gets a unique _id automatically. If you know SQL, these words match like this:

SQLMongoDBIn Mongoose
tablecollectionModel
rowdocumentmodel instance
columnfieldschema path
primary key_idadded automatically

Mongoose: schemas and models

MongoDB itself lets you save any shape of document. Mongoose is a package that adds structure. You describe your data with a schema: field names, types and rules such as required, min, default, trim and lowercase. Then mongoose.model('Student', schema) creates a model, which is the object you use to read and write data. Mongoose names the collection by making the model name lowercase and plural: Student becomes students.

Install it with npm install mongoose. The demo below needs no database. It only checks the data against the schema, so you can try it anywhere. Notice how trim and lowercase clean the input, how default fills a missing value, and how validation reports every broken rule.

blocks.output:
Ayesha ayesha@lgu.edu.pk 18
valid? true
[ 'name', 'age' ]
Path `name` is required.
Path `age` (10) is less than minimum allowed value (16).
students

blocks.html:
Connecting and doing CRUD

To save data you connect with mongoose.connect(url). The URL names the server and the database, for example mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/school. A free hosted database from MongoDB Atlas gives you a similar URL that you keep in .env. Every model method returns a promise, so use await.

TaskMongoose method
CreateModel.create(data)
Read manyModel.find(filter)
Read oneModel.findById(id)
UpdateModel.findByIdAndUpdate(id, data, { new: true })
DeleteModel.findByIdAndDelete(id)

The option { new: true } makes update return the document after the change. This demo needs a MongoDB server running on your computer, so the output below is what you should see with a fresh, empty database.

blocks.output:
Created: Ayesha 19
Has _id: true
Age 20 or more: [ 'Bilal' ]
Updated age: 20
Students left: 1

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Forgetting await on find or create. You get a query or a Promise, not data.
  • Starting the server before the database is connected.
  • Writing the database password in the code. Keep the connection string in .env.
  • Expecting a schema to reject extra fields. By default Mongoose silently ignores fields that are not in the schema.

Key Points

  • MongoDB stores documents in collections; each has a unique _id.
  • A Mongoose schema defines fields and rules; a model gives you the database methods.
  • create, find, findById, findByIdAndUpdate, findByIdAndDelete cover CRUD.
  • All database calls are asynchronous: use await.

topics.title: Authentication: bcrypt, JWT, httpOnly cookies, protecting routes, .env

blocks.html:
Authentication: bcrypt, JWT, httpOnly cookies, protecting routes, .env

Never store plain passwords

Authentication means proving who you are. The first rule: never save a real password in your database. If the database leaks, every user is in danger. Instead save a hash. A hash is a one-way scramble of the password. You cannot turn it back into the password, but you can check a new password against it.

The bcrypt package does this well. bcrypt.hash(password, 10) creates a hash; the number 10 is the cost, which makes guessing slow. bcrypt adds a random salt for you, so two users with the same password get different hashes. bcrypt.compare(password, hash) returns true or false.

JSON Web Tokens (JWT)

After a correct login, the server gives the client a token so the user does not have to send the password again. A JWT has three parts separated by dots: a header, a payload (data such as the user id) and a signature. The server creates the signature with a secret key. Anyone can read the payload, so never put passwords in it. But nobody can change the payload without the signature breaking.

jwt.sign(payload, secret, { expiresIn }) makes a token and jwt.verify(token, secret) checks it. Verify throws an error if the signature is wrong or the token has expired. In this demo we fix the time (iat and clockTimestamp) so the output is always the same. You normally do not need these.

blocks.output:
Hash starts with: $2b$10$
Hash length: 60
Same password? true
Wrong password? false
Parts in token: 3
{ id: 'u1', role: 'student', iat: 1700000000, exp: 1700000900 }
JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature
TokenExpiredError: jwt expired

blocks.html:
httpOnly cookies and protecting routes

Where should the client keep the token? If you put it in localStorage, any script on the page can read it. A safer choice is a cookie with the httpOnly flag. The browser sends it automatically with each request, but JavaScript on the page cannot read it. Add sameSite: 'strict' to reduce cross-site attacks, and secure: true in production so it is sent only over HTTPS. Install cookie-parser so Express fills req.cookies.

To protect a route, write a middleware (like in the middleware lesson). It reads the token from the cookie, verifies it, saves the user in req.user and calls next(). If anything is wrong it answers 401 (not logged in). Then put it in front of any route: app.get('/profile', protect, handler).

Keeping secrets in .env

The secret key must never be written inside your code or pushed to Git. Put it in a file called .env, with lines like JWT_SECRET=some-long-random-text, and add .env to .gitignore. Node 20.6 and newer can load it with node --env-file=.env app.js. Then read values with process.env.JWT_SECRET. The same place is good for your database URL.

The demo uses a fixed user for simplicity. In a real app you would find the user in MongoDB and use bcrypt.compare. Watch the four requests: no cookie, wrong password, correct login, and then the cookie (saved by curl in jar.txt) opening the protected route.

blocks.output:
# Terminal 1 (server)
$ node --env-file=.env app.js
Auth server on 3000

# Terminal 2 (client)
$ curl -s -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/profile'
{"error":"Please log in"}  [401]
$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"ali","password":"wrong"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/login
{"error":"Invalid credentials"}  [401]
$ curl -s -c jar.txt -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"ali","password":"pass123"}' -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:3000/login
{"message":"Logged in"}  [200]
$ curl -s -b jar.txt -w '  [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:3000/profile'
{"hello":"ali"}  [200]

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Saving plain passwords, or hashing with a fast hash like plain SHA instead of bcrypt.
  • Putting the JWT secret in the code or in Git.
  • Telling the user whether the username or the password was wrong. Use one message: "Invalid credentials".
  • Storing sensitive data in a JWT payload. It is readable by anyone.
  • Forgetting cookieParser(), so req.cookies is empty.

Key Points

  • Hash passwords with bcrypt.hash and check with bcrypt.compare.
  • A JWT is signed, not secret: jwt.sign to create, jwt.verify to check.
  • Store the token in an httpOnly cookie.
  • A protect middleware returns 401 or calls next().
  • Keep secrets in .env and out of Git.
